newsitem.title: USA: Drug trial, new surgery featured at heart meeting. [CORRECTED 23:59 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Drug trial, new surgery featured at heart meeting. [CORRECTED 23:59 GMT]

text.p: Results from a huge trial testing a new heart drug, studies on blood clot fighters and minimally invasive heart surgery will be featured at next week's annual meeting of the American Heart Association.

The assocation said it expects over 33,000 cardiologists, scientists and other health care workers to attend its four-day scientific sessions starting Sunday in New Orleans. Some 360 companies will be discussing their cardiovascular drugs and devices at the meeting.
One of the features of the meeting will be a study unveiled Wednesday involving 19,000 patients across 16 countries testing the effect of the drug clopidogrel versus aspirin.
A spokeswoman for Bristol-Myers Squibb Co, which is co-developing clopidogrel with France's Sanofi, described the trial as largest ever done on a drug in development.
(Corrects name of company to Sanofi from Elf Sanofi SA. Corrects to make clear Bristol-Myers Squibb Co is co-developing clopidogrel with Sanofi, not licencing the drug from the French company.)
Pharmaceutical industry analysts said the trial is particularily difficult because it is testing the drug against an active ingredient, aspirin, rather than against a placebo.
It is also testing its ability to prevent three conditions -- heart attack, stroke and periperhal vascular disease -- better than aspirin.
"If the results are very robust, it's all the more significant because the study was such a hard one to do," said Stephen Scala at Cowen and Co.
If the study does show strong results, analysts said they expect Bristol-Myers to file clopidogrel for U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval in early 1997.
Merck and Co Inc and Bristol-Myers have used the American Heart Association forum to unveil blockbuster studies on the benefits of cholesterol-lowering drugs.

Boosted by the studies, sales of Merck's cholesterol-lowerer Zocor rose 47 percent to almost $2.0 billion in the first nine months of 1996, while Bristol-Myers's Pravachol jumped 38 percent to $767 million.
Further studies on the cholesterol-lowering drugs are due to be presented at the conference.
Among biotechnology features at the meeting will be six-month data on a trial of Centocor Inc's blood-clot fighting drug ReoPro.
Interventional cardiologists, with a traditional preference to devices over drugs, have been slow in adopting the drug since its launch in early 1995, analysts said.
The study on the drug's use in patients receiving angioplasty could help Centocor, and its ReoPro partner Eli Lilly and Co, sway doctors, analysts said.

"As the data comes out more and more, and is more and more powerfully in Centocor's favor, I think it will be tough for anybody to argue" against the drug, said Lisa Tuckerman, a biotechnology analyst at Spears, Benzak, Salomon and Farrell.
Data on a rival blood-clot fighting drug, COR Therapeutics Inc and Schering-Plough Corp's Integrelin, will also be presented at the conference.
Cardiologists will also be shown studies on a new technique known as minimally invasive heart surgery, in which surgeons work through small holes in the chest, instead of cutting the chest open.
Companies working in the field include Heartport Inc, CardioThoracic Systems Inc and Medtronic Inc.
--New York Newsdesk, 212-859-1733
